records.name: Delhi
records.current_summary: Region research direction: worse than national on profiling; simultaneously the best-served city in the country for a visitor. (1) Delhi police apprehended four alleged "Bangladeshi nationals disguised as transgender people" from a market area and handed them to the foreigner-registration authority for deportation, with the official framing linking them to begging at traffic signals — the same "transgender = disguise/illegal migrant/begging" police script documented in Tripura and West Bengal, three states apart, meaning it is replicating in the capital. For a foreign visitor this means visible gender-nonconformity in public can be, in Delhi, an independently sufficient reason for a police interaction. (2) At the same time Delhi is the country's most institutionally visible trans city: the longest-running pride marches and the capital's welfare and legal machinery mean a visitor has the deepest support infrastructure here. Both facts coexist. National backdrop from this record's sources: parliament passed a 2026 amendment bill removing the right to self-identification (recognition limited to traditionally accepted socio-cultural groups and intersex people, mandatory medical certification, new offences of "coercion/allurement" punishable with up to life), prompting nationwide protests and a Supreme Court panel's withdrawal call; the national census recorded 487,803 trans persons, only about 32,500 with identity cards.

sources.claim: International human rights organisation news analysis (26 Mar 2026): parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, 2026 — removes the right to self-identification, limits legal recognition to traditionally accepted socio-cultural groups (hijra, kinner) and intersex people, mandates medical certification, and introduces offences of "coercing or alluring" with up to life imprisonment; effectively reverses the 2014 NALSA self-determination ruling; protest held in the capital 25 March 2026; last census recorded 487,803 trans persons, only ~32,500 identity cards issued.

Public broadcaster news report (26 Mar 2026): the amendment bill cleared both houses of parliament and awaits presidential assent; narrows recognition to biological/physical traits, intersex variations and traditional community identities; mandatory medical-board and district-authority certification for gender-affirming surgery; ~2 million trans people estimated in the country; multiple rallies against the bill; Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel urged withdrawal; opposition and trans activists call it an attack on privacy, dignity and the 2014 ruling.

records.name: Seoul
records.current_summary: Region research direction: worse than its reputation — the capital's own council has twice voted to delete anti-discrimination protection, and Pride is contested by the city. (1) 26 April 2024: the Seoul Metropolitan Council passed a bill abolishing the Seoul Student Human Rights Ordinance — 12 years after its promulgation — which had prohibited teachers from discriminating on grounds including gender, sexual orientation and gender identity; the council is controlled by the conservative governing party; abolition triggered protests, the identical bill has now passed a second time and the matter is before the Supreme Court; UN special procedures transmitted a communication on the repeal, with education offices filing observations as enforcing authorities. (2) Pride as contested civic space: the city's mayor uses municipal power against LGBTQ+ gatherings, and the city hosted a mass anti-LGBTQ+ rally claiming 1.1 million participants (organisers, police estimates lower) — described as the largest religious gathering in the country's history. Counterweight: the opposition parliamentary majority announced national student-rights legislation overriding regional offices' decisions, so the repeal is contested and may be undone at national level. Courts from this record's sources: (a) the Seoul Central District Court held that police advice telling a trans person mid-registration-change to "avoid public restrooms for a while" infringed personal rights, awarding 300,000 won (about $240) of a 3 million won claim, final 2 July 2024, calling comfortable restroom use "a fundamental and universal human right"; a national human rights commission survey (2021, 591 trans respondents) found 41% had used a restroom of a different gender than their identity out of fear of unfair treatment, 39% avoided food and drink to avoid restrooms and 36% went without; a 2021 regional district court awarded 7 million won in damages against a beauty academy that barred a trans student's restroom use; (b) a regional court approved gender change for five transgender people without reassignment surgery (8 May 2024), holding that mandatory surgery violates bodily integrity and downgrading prior surgical guidelines to reference status. Model-estimate residual (route 3): largest scene in the country, court protection of the annual queer festival.

sources.claim: National English daily (22 Jul 2024): Seoul Central District Court ruled that a police officer's advice to a transgender person undergoing legal gender change — "avoid using public restrooms for a while" — infringed personal rights, awarding 300,000 won (about $240) of a 3 million won claim, final 2 July; the court called the right to comfortably use restrooms "a fundamental and universal human right" and found the officer should have offered alternatives instead. Also reports a 2021 NHRCK survey (591 trans respondents: 41% used another-gender restroom out of fear, 39% avoided food/drink, 36% skipped restroom use) and a 2021 Daegu District Court (Pohang branch) ruling awarding 7 million won against a beauty academy that barred a trans student's restroom use.

National news agency wire (8 May 2024): a regional court in Yeongdong approved gender change for five transgender people without sex-reassignment surgery, ruling that requiring surgery would force people to violate their own physical integrity; prior court guidelines requiring surgery and proof of infertility are downgraded to reference-only status, though some courts still rely on them to dismiss applications; the case is expected to set precedent.

records.name: Selangor
records.current_summary: Worse than national despite the most 'progressive-governed' appearance: the wealthiest, most urbanised state wrapping the federal capital is not a safe harbour. In January 2026 the state government declared it 'will not allow LGBT promotion' and called for an investigation into a 'Glamping with Pride' gathering; in December 2025 the state's sultan used Friday sermons across state mosques to warn Muslims against LGBT practices — the monarchy-plus-religious-bureaucracy channel operating statewide. The state's religious department is the agency that pursued a well-known transgender entrepreneur with an arrest warrant and an all-out manhunt over her presentation, mobilising 122 religious affairs officers, which made this state the most visible arena for cross-dressing enforcement nationally. Countervailing: it also has the strongest documented prosecution record for violence against trans people — after a 32-year-old trans woman was beaten to death in Klang in 2018, four suspects were arrested and charged. Scored relative to the national score (0.16) for Malaysia.

records.name: Johor
records.current_summary: Worse than national — a state-funded conversion infrastructure. Singapore's commuter twin, the country's most cosmopolitan Malay-majority city (Johor Bahru), directly across the border from a wealthy city-state. In February 2025 the state established an RM400,000 centre to 'rehabilitate' members of deviant groups and people in same-sex relationships, described by the state Islamic religious affairs committee chairman as for individuals with 'distorted' beliefs and those convicted by the syariah court for same-sex relationships, 'to help them resume a normal life'. Independent ethnographic research documents how trans women across the country are channelled into state and religious-institution 'moral reform' programmes aimed at 'rehabilitating' LGBTQ+ Muslims — the rehabilitation apparatus is real, funded, and reaches trans women specifically. Scored relative to the national score (0.16) for Malaysia.

records.name: Malacca
records.current_summary: Worse than national, not 'more relaxed': the state's Islamic religious department detained a 25-year-old man dressed and behaving like a woman while he was doing a TikTok livestream in Banda Hilir in the early hours — a state religious agency acting against public gender expression as such, in a state whose tourism brand is heritage-city strolling (the Peranakan heritage core). The national framework applies unchanged here: same-sex conduct criminalised with up to 20 years and whipping, no legal gender recognition, enforcement routed through state religious-offence laws. records.name: Lima
records.current_summary: Worse than national — the top homicide venue in the state's own data, and the site of 2025 killings. The Public Ministry's study of LGTB homicides 2012–2021 identified 84 criminal complaints, 88 victims and 72 identified perpetrators, and found 58% of the deaths occurred in six fiscal districts, led by Lima (12) and La Libertad (10), with Lima Norte among them; Lima Centro also concentrates the highest national frequency of reported crimes overall (10.0%; eleven fiscal districts hold 62%). On 24–28 August 2025 a trans woman reported missing in Independencia (northern Lima) was found dead in her own home four days later; market colleagues and relatives publicly demanded justice. On the law side, congress approved a norm in February 2025 restricting trans people's access to public bathrooms — analysed by a national human-rights institute as 'legalised discrimination' — and a 2024 rights-observatory report counted 54 LGBTI+ murders 2020–2023, with trans women most affected. Scored relative to the national score (0.36) for Peru.

sources.claim: Infobae Perú (20 February 2025): congress approves a norm that strikes against trans people's right to use public bathrooms; interviews with an LGBTIQ rights activist describing the measure as an attack on trans people's access to public space.

IDEHPUCP human-rights institute bulletin, 'Discriminación legalizada': analysis of congress's prohibition on trans people accessing public bathrooms, characterised as legalised discrimination with public-space consequences.

Agencia Presentes (22 July 2024): hate crimes rose — 54 LGBTI+ people were murdered 2020–2023 according to the annual report of the LGBTI+ human-rights observatory of a Peruvian university, with trans women the most affected.

records.name: Ankara
records.current_summary: Model estimate (route 3, best-knowledge delta): capital — diplomatic bubble; a standing gubernatorial ban on public LGBTI activities (2017-2019 legacy); at the 22 June 2024 Pride attempt police blocked the march, activists read their statement and dispersed peacefully. National frame: a leaked October 2025 draft judicial package would criminalise 'conduct contrary to biological sex' and its promotion (up to 3 years), restrict gender-affirming care (minimum age 25) and expose providers, support groups and journalists to charges; a 2025 national rights report records hostility institutionalised as explicit state policy, six violations of the right to life with trans people most affected, and expression and artistic freedom restricted. Scored relative to the national score (0.15) for Turkey.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (29 Oct 2025): a leaked '11th Judicial Package' would amend the penal and civil codes with articles threatening LGBT people — behaviour 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' and its 'promotion' (up to three years' prison, amending the indecent-acts provision); sharp restrictions on gender-affirming care (minimum age 25, onerous eligibility); potential charges against trans people, care providers, civil-society organisations and journalists; justified as protecting 'the family and public morals'.

Kaos GL's LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025, 'The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People': hostility institutionalised as explicit state policy — presidency-centred targeting, the family ministry as implementing body, religious-broadcast regulator and content restrictions on expression and artistic freedom, one LGBTI+ organisation closed, digital-platform penalties and broadcast censorship; six violations of the right to life documented (three recorded as hate-motivated), trans people the most affected; no state hate-crime statistics exist so data rests on media reporting. Launched at a public event in the capital.
